Score breakdown: constitutional_recognition: 1/3 (1 provisions found); dedicated_legislation: 4/4 (3 laws found); institutional_mechanisms: 3/3 (3 mechanisms found); judicial_enforcement: 1/2 (1 precedents found); international_leadership: 2/2 (2 commitments found); policy_integration: 2/2 (3 integration points found). Strongest documented sections: dedicated_legislation (3), institutional_mechanisms (3), policy_integration (3). Analyst notes: Australia presents a dynamic and evolving picture. Its strongest asset is the EPBC Act's statutory intergenerational equity principle — one of the most explicit in the common law world — which applies to all national environmental decisions. The Sharma case was a near-miss: the first global judicial finding of a ministerial duty of care to future generations (overturned on appeal), but it accelerated climate litigation globally. The Wellbeing of Future Generations Bill 2025 is the most significant current development — a direct attempt to replicate Wales' WFGA with active civil society backing and a cross-party parliamentary group. The mandatory Intergenerational Report (40-year fiscal horizon) and the Measuring What Matters framework show growing policy integration. The main gap is a lack of constitutional recognition and the absence of a statutory future generations commissioner — both of which the 2025 Bill would address if passed.. Strongest documented sections: dedicated_legislation (4), institutional_mechanisms (4), international_commitments (3). Analyst notes: The UK presents a mixed picture. Wales is a global leader with its Well-being of Future Generations Act and Commissioner — the only country with such a comprehensive legal framework. However, at the UK-wide level, there is no codified constitution, no dedicated future generations legislation (two bills failed to progress), and no national commissioner. The UK's strength lies in its climate governance infrastructure (Climate Change Act, CCC, carbon budgets) and fiscal long-term analysis (OBR), which indirectly serve intergenerational equity. The House of Lords committee's 2019 recommendations for Intergenerational Impact Assessments remain unimplemented. UK courts have been reluctant to enforce international climate obligations domestically (FoE v UKEF), limiting judicial enforcement of intergenerational climate duties.. Analyst notes: India has one of the stronger constitutional-environmental doctrines in the Global South, even without a standalone future generations act. Its framework rests on a mix of constitutional duties, expansive Article 21 jurisprudence, core environmental statutes, and a specialized environmental tribunal. The strongest recent development is the Supreme Court's 2024 recognition that protection against the adverse effects of climate change flows from Articles 14 and 21. That said, India still lacks a dedicated future generations commissioner or ombudsperson, and the implementation gap is substantial: environmental clearances remain contested, ecological protection is often traded against development imperatives, and intergenerational fairness is not yet systematically embedded in fiscal, youth-participation, or whole-of-government decision processes. In other words, India is doctrinally ambitious but institutionally uneven.. Strongest documented sections: international_commitments (3), constitutional_provisions (2), dedicated_legislation (2). Analyst notes: Italy's headline story is its landmark 2022 constitutional amendment — one of the first countries globally to insert 'future generations' explicitly into the fundamental principles of its constitution (Article 9). This gives the concept constitutional standing at the highest level of the legal order. The judicial picture is nascent but active: the Giudizio Universale case (2024) was dismissed on procedural grounds but used Article 9's future generations language, and the ENI case is proceeding after Supreme Court confirmed jurisdiction in 2025. The main gaps are the absence of a dedicated national institution (no commissioner or ombudsperson) and no specific implementing legislation for the Article 9 mandate beyond the NRRP. Italy also benefits from EU-level architecture — the EU's new Intergenerational Fairness Commissioner and EU Climate Law both strengthen Italy's framework from above..
